title: Nostra Aetate and religious freedom
hook: the Church rejects blaming the Jewish people for Christ's death and affirms religious freedom (Dignitatis Humanae)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pastoral Constitution, and your line: their joys are ours. The council claimed the world's joys and griefs as its own. Now, two harder questions: its Jewish neighbors, and freedom of conscience. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

In our time. That's all the Latin title means: Nostra Aetate. Two plain words to open a short text in which the council asks how Catholics should speak about other religions, and, in one section, about Jews. Beside it the council set another text, on religious freedom, called Dignitatis Humanae, the dignity of the human person. One looks at an old wrong. The other looks at every conscience. Today: Nostra Aetate and religious freedom.
screen: `IN OUR TIME.` → `AN OLD WRONG, A NEW TEACHING.` → `NOSTRA AETATE AND RELIGIOUS FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Start with Nostra Aetate. In its section on the Jewish people, the council remembers the spiritual bond that ties the Church to Abraham's descendants. It says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews living then, without distinction, nor against the Jews of today. It says the Jews must not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if scripture taught that. And it says the Church deplores hatred, persecution and displays of antisemitism directed against Jews at any time and by anyone. It grounds this in Saint Paul, who wrote of the Jewish people, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance." The council reads it to mean God does not take his gifts back. Then, Dignitatis Humanae. Its claim fits in a sentence. Every human person has a right to religious freedom. No one may be forced to act against their conscience in religious matters, and no one may be stopped from acting by it, within just limits, alone or with others. The council roots this not in politics but in the dignity of the person. And it adds a point from inside the faith itself: the act of faith, it says, has to be free. Nobody can be forced into believing. Both documents ask Catholics to look honestly at the past and to treat every neighbor, of any faith or none, as a person whose conscience is their own. Catholics have kept working out what these texts mean, in study and in dialogue. That's today's line: no one may be forced.
screen: `A BOND WITH ABRAHAM'S PEOPLE.` · `NO BLAME ON ALL JEWS.` · `HATRED DEPLORED.` · `FREEDOM OF CONSCIENCE FOR ALL.` · then, large: `NO ONE MAY BE FORCED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Jewish neighbors. For the sit, bring to mind a Jewish person or community you know, or a synagogue you pass, or simply the Jewish people around the world. Hold them with good will: their safety, their families, their Sabbath, their joy. If you pray, you can ask God to bless them and to guard them from hatred. If you don't, simply wish them well, and mean it. The bell holds the time.
Nostra Aetate. The council's rejection of blaming the Jewish people for Christ's death, read alongside its teaching that every conscience is free. Today's word.
Your line: no one may be forced. Today, when you disagree with someone about faith, say your piece, and leave their conscience in their own hands. Day seven hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholic dioceses and the Holy See hold ongoing dialogue with Jewish communities, Catholic teaching rejects antisemitism and any blame of the Jewish people for Christ's death, and the Church teaches that faith must be freely accepted.

original.note: Latin, in our time: the document's first words, which became its name.

what a scholar hears: both grounded in scripture and human dignity: Romans 11:29 for the Jewish people, and the freedom of the act of faith.
